title: Shoftim: even the king reads (Deuteronomy 17:18–20)
hook: the king writes his own copy of the Torah so his heart isn't lifted up
tomorrow: Shoftim: is the tree a man? (Deuteronomy 20:19)

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzedek tzedek tirdof: pursue justice, and pursue it justly. Your line was justice, justice. Was the way you argued fair? Today, the law for the most powerful person in the land. Day five hundred four.

In the ancient world, a king was the law. His word settled things. His image was on the coins. Scribes wrote down his victories and carved them into stone. The idea that a king might have to sit down with a pen and copy out somebody else's law, by hand, every word, and then read it every day of his life, would have sounded absurd in most royal courts. Deuteronomy's chapter on kings is short, and it's mostly a list of limits. And it ends with homework.
screen: `THE KING WAS THE LAW.` → `COPY SOMEONE ELSE'S LAW?` → `A CHAPTER OF LIMITS.`

segments.voice: First the limits. If Israel sets a king over itself, he must not pile up horses, or take many wives, or heap up silver and gold. Power, pleasure, money: the three things kings usually collect. Then the homework. In the old Jewish translation: when he sits on his throne, "he shall write him a copy of this law in a book." And it shall be with him, "and he shall read therein all the days of his life." Why? The verse says it plainly: "that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren." Brothers. The king is still one of them. The Talmud, in Sanhedrin, adds that the king actually writes a scroll of his own, kept with him wherever he goes, even into battle. And it notes that every Jew is commanded to write a Torah scroll; the king just has an extra one. The phrase for a copy of this law is mishneh hatorah. It's where Deuteronomy gets its Greek name, second law. And over a thousand years later, Maimonides borrowed the same words for his great law code, the Mishneh Torah. The king reading every day is a picture of power under something bigger than itself. Not the king's word over the law, but the law over the king's word. Reading isn't a reward for the powerful. It's a brake.
screen: `NOT HORSES, WIVES, OR GOLD.` · `WRITE HIM A COPY OF THIS LAW.` · `NOT LIFTED ABOVE HIS BROTHERS.` · `MISHNEH TORAH: SECOND LAW.` · then, large: `EVEN THE KING READS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a line that humbles you. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place where you have some power. A parent, a manager, the one who knows the most in the room, the oldest sibling. Now think of a line, from scripture, from a teacher, from your grandmother, that puts that power back in its place. Something like: you are one of them. If you can, find it and read it now, slowly, twice. Let it sit above you for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Shoftim. Judges. The portion where even the king must write the law down and read it every day.

Your line: even the king reads. A week of tzedakah, the release, simcha, giving by your blessing, judges at the gates, and justice twice. Today, read your humbling line again before you use any power you have. Day five hundred four.

howItsDone: Jewish law counts writing a Torah scroll as a commandment for every Jew; many fulfill it today by sponsoring or writing a single letter in a community's new scroll, and the king's special scroll is discussed in the Talmud and Maimonides.

fork.setup: you've just been crowned king of Israel. what's the first thing Deuteronomy tells you to do on your throne?
options: write a copy of the law for yourself, and read it daily.
fork.reveal: he shall write him a copy of this law in a book, and read therein all the days of his life.

original.note: Hebrew: a copy, or repetition, of the law. the source of Deuteronomy's Greek name, and of Maimonides' Mishneh Torah.

trapdoor: what you thought: kings should be educated.
what it means: the most powerful person writes out and reads a law above himself, so he stays one of his brothers.
what a scholar hears: Sanhedrin 21b gives the king his own scroll beside the one every Jew must write; mishneh hatorah becomes Deuteronomy and Maimonides' code.
